description: For more than three thousand years, the civilization along the Nile produced art devoted to kingship, the gods and the afterlife. Egyptian artists worked within remarkably stable conventions: figures shown in composite profile, hierarchical scale, and hieroglyphic inscriptions that were as much image as text. Much of what survives comes from tombs, where objects were meant to serve the dead for eternity. The collection spans the New Kingdom to the Roman period, from cosmetic items such as a kohl container shaped like a palm column and a bronze hand mirror to ushabti figurines, amulets of Isis and Horus, a statuette of Osiris and a cat coffin reflecting animal cults. Painted Fayum portraits, such as Portrait of a Man Wearing an Ivy Wreath, show how Egyptian burial customs merged with Greco-Roman realism.

Ancient Greek art laid many foundations of the Western tradition, from the idealized human figure to the orders of classical architecture. Pottery offers an especially rich record: Corinthian workshops of the 7th century BCE decorated small oil flasks with animal friezes, while Athenian potters perfected black-figure and then red-figure painting, depicting myths, athletics and daily life. The collection includes Athenian vases attributed to named hands such as the Achilles Painter and the Chicago Painter, a painter named after a vase in this museum, as well as wares made in the Greek cities of southern Italy, like Apulian drinking cups. Silver coins minted in Thebes, Knossos and elsewhere carry the images of gods and civic emblems, and Hellenistic gold jewelry shows the refined craftsmanship of the period after Alexander the Great.

Before Rome dominated the Mediterranean, the Etruscans of central Italy developed a vibrant culture of their own, visible here in a votive terracotta head from around 500 BCE. Roman art absorbed Etruscan and especially Greek traditions, copying famous Greek statues and adapting them for villas, gardens and public spaces; the collection's Statue of the Aphrodite of Knidos and Statue of Meleager are Roman versions of celebrated Greek originals. Romans also prized realistic portraiture as a means of commemoration and political messaging. Portrait heads of Emperor Hadrian and his favorite Antinous reflect imperial taste of the 2nd century, while gold and silver coins portraying Julius Caesar, Otho, Antoninus Pius, Caracalla and Aurelian served as portable propaganda, carrying the ruler's likeness throughout the empire.

Long before European contact, the Americas were home to sophisticated civilizations that produced monumental architecture, intricate textiles, ceramics and metalwork. Art often served ritual and political purposes, linking rulers to deities, ancestors and the cycles of agriculture. The collection ranges from a mural fragment from the great city of Teotihuacan and lively ceramic figures from West Mexico, such as the Jalisco Storyteller, to Maya painted vessels, including one signed by the painter Aj Maxam, and a scene of a ballgame player. Aztec (Mexica) sculpture is represented by the Coronation Stone of Moctezuma Xocoyotzin and a head of the maize goddess Xilonen. Gold pendants from Coclé in Panama, a Chimú ceremonial knife from Peru, and Ancestral Puebloan pottery from the American Southwest show the breadth of these traditions.

The arts of Africa encompass an enormous diversity of cultures, each with its own forms, materials and meanings. Many works were created to be used: masks performed in masquerades, figures that honored ancestors or embodied spiritual power, and finely carved furnishings that signaled status. Sculptors often worked within established styles while bringing individual invention, and some, like the Yoruba carver Abogunde of Ede, are known by name. The collection includes a Kongo power figure (nkisi nkondi) studded with nails, a Chokwe chihongo mask, a Fang reliquary head from Gabon, a Luluwa mother-and-child figure, a Zulu headrest and a Swahili chair from Lamu. A portrait figure of a Bangwa king from Cameroon and a terracotta equestrian group from Mali, made centuries earlier, show the depth of the continent's artistic history.

The arts of China, Korea and Japan share deep connections, including the spread of Buddhism and a high regard for calligraphy, ceramics and bronze. In China, ritual bronzes of the Zhou dynasty gave way to refined Tang dynasty sculpture and glazed ceramics, such as the collection's dragon-handled amphora, and to Song dynasty tea wares and serene images of the bodhisattva Guanyin. Korea's Goryeo potters became renowned for celadon, seen in a duck-shaped ewer. Japanese art ranges from powerful Kamakura-period Buddhist guardians like Shukongojin and Fudō Myō-ō to Oribe ceramics made for the tea ceremony. Edo-period woodblock prints by Katsushika Hokusai and Utagawa Hiroshige, with their bold design and vivid storytelling, later had a profound influence on European artists.

The art of South and Southeast Asia is inseparable from the religious traditions of Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism, which spread across the region and shaped its temples, sculpture and painting. Images of deities follow detailed iconographic rules, with multiple arms, attributes and gestures (mudras) that identify each figure and its powers. The collection's earliest work, Goddess Hariti Seated Holding a Child, comes from Gandhara in present-day Pakistan, where Greco-Roman and Indian styles met. South Indian bronzes of the Chola period, including Shiva as Lord of the Dance (Nataraja) and a meditating Buddha from Nagapattinam, are among the finest metal sculptures ever made. Stone figures of Shiva and Uma, Sarasvati and Karttikeya, and an Angkor-period Shiva from the Mekong Delta, show the tradition's reach.

Islamic art refers to the art produced in lands where Islam was the dominant religion or culture, stretching from Spain to Central Asia and India. It is not only religious: much of it was made for palaces, homes and markets. Because figural imagery was avoided in religious contexts, artists developed extraordinary traditions of calligraphy, geometric pattern and vegetal ornament, known as arabesque, though figures appear often in secular objects. Ceramics were a particular strength. The collection's Bowl with Calligraphic Design, made in 10th-century eastern Iran or Central Asia under the Samanids, uses elegant Arabic script as its sole decoration, while an Inscribed Mina'i Bowl from Seljuq Iran features colorful enameled figures. A Safavid ewer and a bracelet from Mamluk-era Egypt round out this small group.

Medieval art spans more than a thousand years, from the founding of Constantinople to the dawn of the Renaissance. In the Byzantine East, mosaics, icons and coinage expressed the union of church and empire; the collection includes an early mosaic fragment of a man leading a giraffe and a gold solidus of Empress Irene. In Western Europe, art centered on the church. Romanesque workshops produced precious reliquaries, such as a casket from León in Spain, while the Gothic era brought soaring cathedrals, carved stone sculpture like the Head of an Apostle from Paris, and painted altarpieces. Late Gothic painters such as Lorenzo Monaco in Florence and Bernat Martorell in Catalonia, whose Saint George and the Dragon glows with gold and jewel-like color, bridge the medieval and Renaissance worlds.

The Renaissance, meaning rebirth, began in 15th-century Italy as artists and scholars revived the learning of classical antiquity. Painters developed linear perspective, studied anatomy and sought naturalistic space and light, while patrons like the Medici funded ambitious commissions. In Northern Europe, painters such as Rogier van der Weyden perfected oil paint to render astonishing detail, and Albrecht Dürer brought Italian ideas to German printmaking, as in Knight, Death, and the Devil. The collection includes devotional works by Sandro Botticelli and Correggio, as well as works by Giovanni di Paolo, Jean Hey and Alessandro Vittoria. Mannerism, which emerged in the 16th century, favored elongated figures, complex poses and heightened emotion, qualities pushed to an extreme by El Greco in Spain, whose Assumption of the Virgin is a highlight here.

Baroque art emerged around 1600 in Rome and spread across Europe, marked by drama, movement, strong contrasts of light and shadow, and an appeal to the emotions. In Catholic countries it served the Counter-Reformation, filling churches with persuasive, theatrical imagery; Peter Paul Rubens in Flanders was its most energetic exponent, and Diego Velázquez in Spain brought a sober naturalism, as in his early Kitchen Scene. In the Protestant Dutch Republic, a thriving market for paintings led artists such as Jan Steen, Pieter Codde and Jacob Ochtervelt to specialize in genre scenes, landscapes and still lifes for middle-class homes. The style culminated in the airy, luminous decorative painting of Giovanni Battista Tiepolo, whose Rinaldo and Armida canvases in this collection mark the late, lighter phase of the Baroque.

In the early 18th century, the grandeur of the Baroque gave way to the Rococo, a lighter, more playful style favored in French aristocratic interiors. Artists such as François Boucher painted pastoral love scenes in soft pastel tones, while cabinetmakers and porcelain factories like Sèvres produced curving, elaborately ornamented furnishings and wares. In Venice, Francesco Guardi captured the city's shimmering light. By the 1760s, excavations at Herculaneum and Pompeii and Enlightenment ideals inspired a return to classical simplicity. Neoclassicism, led by Jacques-Louis David in France and the sculptor Antonio Canova in Italy, favored clear outlines, balanced compositions and themes of virtue. Hubert Robert's views of ancient ruins and Joshua Reynolds's portrait of Lady Sarah Bunbury sacrificing to the Graces reflect this fascination with antiquity.

Romanticism arose in the late 18th century as a reaction against Enlightenment rationalism and Neoclassical restraint. Romantic artists prized emotion, imagination and individual experience, and they were drawn to the sublime power of nature, to history and literature, and to the exotic and the supernatural. Henry Fuseli explored dreams and literary themes from Milton and Dante, while Francisco Goya created intensely personal and often dark images of Spanish life. In France, Eugène Delacroix championed vivid color and dramatic movement, drawing on Lord Byron and his travels in North Africa. In England, John Constable elevated the everyday landscape, as in Stoke-by-Nayland, and in the United States Thomas Cole founded the Hudson River School, celebrating the American wilderness as a source of national identity and spiritual renewal.

Realism emerged in France in the mid-19th century as artists rejected idealized history painting and romantic fantasy in favor of depicting contemporary life truthfully, including ordinary people, labor and unglamorous subjects. Gustave Courbet was its leading champion, and his Mère Grégoire shows his frank, robust approach. Édouard Manet brought modern Parisian subjects and bold, flattened handling to the Salon, paving the way for Impressionism. In the United States, Winslow Homer and Thomas Eakins developed a powerful native realism, depicting fishermen, athletes and sitters with unflinching observation. Sculptors such as Auguste Rodin and Aimé-Jules Dalou brought new naturalism and emotional intensity to the human figure. Later, Robert Henri and his circle carried Realism's commitment to everyday life into the 20th century with scenes of the modern city.

Impressionism took shape in Paris in the late 1860s, when a group of young painters began working outdoors to capture the fleeting effects of light, weather and atmosphere. Using quick, broken brushstrokes and bright, unmixed colors, they painted modern life: boulevards, railway stations, suburban leisure and the changing countryside. Rejected by the official Salon, they organized eight independent exhibitions between 1874 and 1886; a critic mocking Claude Monet's Impression, Sunrise gave the movement its name. The collection is rich in Monet's work, including his Stacks of Wheat series, alongside paintings by Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Edgar Degas, Camille Pissarro, Alfred Sisley, Berthe Morisot and Gustave Caillebotte, whose Paris Street; Rainy Day is a highlight. Americans such as Mary Cassatt and Childe Hassam carried the style across the Atlantic.

Post-Impressionism describes artists who, building on Impressionism's bright color and modern subjects, sought something more lasting, structured or expressive. The term was coined later by the critic Roger Fry and covers highly individual approaches rather than a unified movement. Georges Seurat applied scientific color theory in tiny dots, as in A Sunday on La Grande Jatte — 1884. Paul Cézanne rebuilt form with patches of color, laying the groundwork for Cubism. Vincent van Gogh used intense color and vigorous brushwork to convey emotion, while Paul Gauguin turned to flat, symbolic color and subjects from Brittany and Tahiti. Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec chronicled the nightlife of Montmartre. Together these artists opened the path to Fauvism, Expressionism and abstraction in the 20th century.

The Arts and Crafts movement began in Britain as a reaction against the poor quality of mass-produced goods in the industrial age. Inspired by writers such as John Ruskin and designer William Morris, it championed honest materials, skilled handwork and the unity of art and everyday life. Art Nouveau, which flourished around 1900, shared the aim of reforming design but embraced sinuous, nature-inspired lines. The collection includes furniture by Edward William Godwin, whose sideboard reflects the Anglo-Japanese taste, M. H. Baillie Scott and Charles Rennie Mackintosh of Glasgow, and a fireplace surround by the Chicago architect George Washington Maher. American silver and glass by Tiffany and Company and Louis Comfort Tiffany's workshops, along with a stoneware jar by the enslaved potter David Drake, broaden the story of American craft.

The art of colonial and early national America reflects the ambitions of a young society. Portraiture was the dominant form of painting, as merchants and their families commissioned likenesses to record status and lineage. John Smibert, trained in Britain, helped establish the tradition in Boston, followed by John Singleton Copley, whose portrait of Mrs. Daniel Hubbard shows his crisp realism. After independence, Gilbert Stuart and Charles Willson Peale portrayed the new nation's leaders and citizens, and Joshua Johnson of Baltimore became one of the first professional African American portrait painters. Craftsmen produced fine silver, like Cornelius Kierstede's two-handled cup, and clocks such as Simon Willard's lighthouse clock. The collection also includes a ceramic chocolate jar from Puebla in New Spain and Alvan Fisher's early landscape The Prairie on Fire.

Modernism describes the wave of experimentation that transformed art in the first half of the 20th century. Rejecting academic conventions and the imitation of nature, artists explored new ways of representing experience, from bold, non-naturalistic color to the fragmentation of form and full abstraction. Henri Matisse led the Fauves in liberating color, while in Germany the Blue Rider circle of Vasily Kandinsky and Franz Marc pursued spiritual expression, as in Kandinsky's Improvisation No. 30 (Cannons). Piet Mondrian reduced painting to lines and primary colors in search of universal harmony. Americans such as Marsden Hartley absorbed these ideas and applied them to American subjects, while Amedeo Modigliani's elongated portraits and Gaston Lachaise's sculpture reinvented the human figure. The collection also includes Narcissa Niblack Thorne's miniature period rooms, created in the 1930s.
